column5: proclaiming the Name; ascribing greatness
column6: 87:1 commands glorification of the Lord's name; Moses says that he will proclaim YHWH's name and calls his hearers to ascribe greatness to God, joining the two acts in one formula.

column5: God Most High; blessing
column6: Melchizedek blesses God Most High after deliverance; the explicit divine title and blessing give a close Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's Lord Most High whose name is glorified.

column5: glory due the Name; offering and worship
column6: The verse moves from giving YHWH the glory due his name to bringing an offering and worshipping, closely matching the commentary's treatment of praise of the Name and formal worship as one practice.

column5: Name, sunrise and sunset, pure offering
column6: Malachi makes YHWH's name great from sunrise to sunset and connects it with incense and a pure offering; it gathers the commentary's daily praise, Name, ritual action, and 14–15 purification link.

column5: Name praised from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary invokes praise before sunrise and before sunset; this verse explicitly makes the praise of YHWH's name extend from the sun's rising to its setting.

column5: blessing the great God; bowing and face-to-ground worship
column6: Ezra blesses YHWH the great God, and the assembly answers, raises hands, bows, and worships with faces to the ground; it is a compact public analogue to praise, utterance, and bodily prayer together.

column5: Torah reading, confession, worship
column6: The people stand to read Torah and then confess and worship; this concretely parallels the commentary's claim that recitation, admonitory remembrance, and prayer belong to the same devotional work.

column5: kneeling, prayer, thanksgiving, three daily times
column6: Daniel kneels three times a day, prays, and gives thanks before his God, furnishing a specific counterpart to prayer as bodily movement, supplication, praise, and a recurring practice.

column5: lips moving; voice unheard; inward prayer
column6: Hannah speaks in her heart while her lips move and her voice is not heard; the contrast supplies a precise counterpart to the commentary's open vocal prayer or recitation and God's knowledge of what is hidden.

column5: bowing and kneeling before the Maker
column6: The psalm's invitation to worship, bow down, and kneel gives named bodily acts corresponding to the commentary's standing, bowing, prostration, and supplication as prayer.

column5: falling on faces; spoken confession of God
column6: The people fall on their faces and voice a confession of YHWH; the verse joins the physical prostration and verbal God-remembrance that the commentary treats as a single act.

column5: holy Name; God sanctifying Israel
column6: The verse forbids profaning the holy Name and calls God the one who sanctifies Israel, sharpening the commentary's 14–15 linkage between a worshipper's prayer and God's purifying action.

column5: purified speech; calling on the Name; united service
column6: God gives peoples a purified lip so that they may call on YHWH's name and serve together; it links the commentary's tongue-bound dhikr, purification, and obedient worship without reducing them to mere speech.

column5: book in the mouth; meditation; doing
column6: Joshua is to keep the Torah-book in his mouth, meditate on it day and night, and do it; this closely parallels the commentary's inclusion of recitation, tongue, intention, and obedient action within remembrance.

column5: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: The covenant song is to remain unforgotten from Israel's mouths; it supplies a concrete scriptural analogue to the commentary's movement from being made to recite to not forgetting and then reminding.

column5: lips honoring God; heart far away
column6: Isaiah distinguishes lip-honor from a distant heart; it illuminates the commentary's insistence that tesbih involves word, action, and intention, and its warning about heedless prayer.

column5: outspread hands; many prayers; violence
column6: God refuses many prayers while the worshippers' hands are full of blood; this gives a pointed ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that prayer turns people away from indecency and wrong.

column5: forced prostration to an image; fiery punishment
column6: The verse orders bodily falling and worship under threat of a burning furnace. Alongside the commentary's prostration as Lord-directed prayer and its fire imagery, it makes the object and moral character of bodily worship decisive.

column5: falling face-down before God Most High
column6: The assembled people fall on their faces to worship the Almighty, God Most High; it brings together the commentary's epithet, public liturgy, and prostrating body.

column5: explicit Name; kneeling, prostration, blessing
column6: On hearing the explicit Name from the high priest, priests and people kneel, prostrate, fall on their faces, and bless the Name; this rabbinic liturgy tightly combines the Name and the bodily acts named in the commentary.

column5: prayer as supplication
column6: Rabbi Eliezer's dictum that a prayer made fixed is not supplication gives a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the commentary's explicit gloss that salat is du'a, while resisting prayer as empty routine.

column5: Hannah's moving lips and unraised voice
column6: The Talmud reads Hannah's silent, lip-moving prayer as a source for how the Amidah is voiced. That interpretation makes the commentary's audible prayer or recitation and its hidden dimension a concrete liturgical question.

column5: blessing the Name at light and darkness
column6: The Rule of the Community schedules blessing God's name at the turning points of light and darkness, a close sectarian-Jewish analogue to the commentary's praise before sunrise and sunset.

column5: magnifying and sanctifying the great Name
column6: Kaddish begins by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified; its congregational formula directly stands beside 87:1's command to glorify the Lord's name.

column5: hallowing the Father's name in prayer
column6: Jesus' model prayer makes the hallowing of God's name its first petition, directly pairing prayer with the treatment of the divine name central to 87:1 and 87:15.

column5: sacrifice of praise; fruit of lips confessing the Name
column6: Hebrews calls continual praise the fruit of lips that confess God's name; it closely matches the commentary's dhikr as the Name on the tongue and tesbih as worship.

column5: praying and singing praise with spirit and mind
column6: Paul deliberately pairs prayer and praise in both spirit and mind, providing a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's unified tesbih, remembrance, and prayer with intentional participation.

column5: prayer, supplication, thanksgiving
column6: Paul joins prayer and supplication with thanksgiving in one act of address to God, closely echoing the commentary's salat as du'a and dhikr as praise and thanks.

column5: praying and hymn-singing heard by others
column6: Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight, with prisoners listening; this is a specific scene of the vocal, audible devotional practice developed from jahr in the commentary.

column5: word dwelling, teaching and admonition, psalms and gratitude
column6: The verse puts instruction and admonition together with psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and gratitude; it closely resembles the commentary's intervening recitation, reminder, and worship as one practice.

column5: presenting bodies as living worship
column6: Paul describes offering bodies as a living sacrifice and worship; it gives a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's claim that worship includes bodily action as well as verbal and intentional devotion.

column5: falling on the face and praying
column6: Jesus falls on his face and prays in Gethsemane, an explicit conjunction of prostrating posture and supplication comparable to the prayer movements named in the commentary.

column5: bodily humility and a plea for mercy
column6: The tax collector stands at a distance, lowers his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy; it supplies a concrete Christian scene in which bodily prayer and du'a-like petition are inseparable.

column5: bowing every knee at a name
column6: In its Christological setting, the verse makes the response to Jesus' name a universal bending of knees; it is a precise Christian meeting of named confession and the bodily prayer emphasized in the commentary.

column5: prayer in secret; the Father seeing the hidden
column6: Jesus directs prayer to the hidden place and grounds it in the Father's seeing what is hidden; this complements 87:7 as read in the commentary, where God knows both vocalized and concealed devotion.

column5: lips honoring God; heart distant
column6: Jesus applies Isaiah's lips-and-heart critique to a dispute about worship and tradition. It provides a Christian interpretive development of the commentary's contrast between tongue-level mention and wholehearted, attentive worship.

column5: calling on the Lord's name and salvation
column6: Paul's citation makes calling on the Lord's name the path to salvation; it gives a specific New Testament meeting with the commentary's sequence of remembering the Name, praying, and flourishing.

column5: threefold holy acclamation; glory filling earth
column6: The seraphim's antiphonal holy acclamation is a heavenly praise formula for YHWH. It offers a liturgical setting for the commentary's tesbih of the transcendent Lord, though it does not reproduce its prayer sequence.

column5: the high and lifted One; holy Name; reviving the lowly
column6: Isaiah calls God high and lifted up, whose name is Holy, and says that he revives the contrite. This joins the Most High epithet to a divine restoring action relevant to the commentary's praise and purification pairing.

column5: Arabic س ب ح (B001); Hebrew שׁבח
column6: The commentary labels Arabic س ب ح as B001. Psalm 117 uses the Hebrew Piel imperative שַׁבְּחוּהוּ, “praise him,” a likely Semitic cognate in a summons for all peoples to praise YHWH.

column5: Arabic ذ ك ر (B004/B005); Hebrew זכר
column6: The commentary labels ذ ك ر as B004/B005 and develops remembering the Lord. Deuteronomy's זכר, “remember,” directs Israel to remember YHWH as the giver of power, a cognate used for faithful recollection rather than merely saying a word.

column5: Arabic ص ل و (B002/B003); Biblical Aramaic מְצַלֵּא
column6: The commentary labels ص ل و as B002/B003. Daniel's Aramaic מְצַלֵּא, “praying,” is a close Aramaic-Syriac cognate form; its repeated kneeling and thanksgiving make the linguistic meeting concrete.

column5: Torah reading, Shema, directing the heart
column6: The Mishnah asks whether someone already reading Torah fulfils the Shema when its time comes, and makes the answer turn on directing the heart. It clarifies the commentary's claim that recitation can be remembrance and worship only with intention.

column5: directing the heart before prayer
column6: The early pietists pause before prayer in order to direct their hearts to their Father in heaven; this gives a concrete rabbinic practice for the commentary's inclusion of intention within tesbih and salat.

column5: patriarchal derivation of fixed prayer times
column6: The Talmud derives the three daily prayer services from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Its interpretive fixing of prayer in the day supplies a Jewish liturgical bridge to the commentary's praise at the sun's turning points.

column5: the ninth-hour time of prayer
column6: Peter and John go up together to the temple at the appointed hour of prayer. The scene offers a specific communal, timed counterpart to the commentary's recurring prayer and praise.

column5: worship in spirit and truth
column6: Jesus identifies true worship with spirit and truth. It gives an interpretive complement to the commentary's refusal to reduce worship to bodily movement or spoken formula, while retaining worship as an enacted practice.

column5: psalms and hymns spoken and sung in the heart
column6: The exhortation joins speaking psalms and hymns with singing in the heart to the Lord; it reflects the commentary's double focus on vocal remembrance and inward devotion.

column5: unceasing prayer
column6: The command to pray without ceasing provides a Christian analogue to the commentary's repeated, abundant tesbih and remembrance, although it does not prescribe the same ritual form.

column5: doing good and sharing as sacrifices pleasing to God
column6: This verse calls concrete beneficence and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God. It extends the commentary's word-action-intention account of worship to an explicitly ethical Christian practice.

column5: confession, forgiveness, cleansing
column6: God forgives and cleanses those who confess; it provides a specific Christian pairing of spoken penitential address and divine purification relevant to the commentary's 14–15 relation.

column5: reciting the Lord's Prayer three times daily
column6: The Didache turns the Lord's Prayer into a thrice-daily discipline. This early Christian rule offers a concrete liturgical counterpart to the commentary's repeated prayer and remembrance around the day.
